source_text: The lemma above can also be proved using the reflection principle. However, one has to be careful. Namely, suppose the sentence <MATH_0001> expresses the property ``<MATH_0002> is a scheme'', then what does the formula <MATH_0003> mean? It is true that the reflection principle says we can find <MATH_0004> such that for all <MATH_0005> we have <MATH_0006> but this is entirely useless. It is only by combining two such statements that something interesting happens. For example suppose <MATH_0007> expresses the property ``<MATH_0008>, <MATH_0009> are schemes, and <MATH_0010> is the reduction of <MATH_0011>'' (see Schemes, Definition <REF_0001>). Suppose we apply the reflection principle to the pair of formulas <MATH_0012>, <MATH_0013>. Then it is easy to see that any <MATH_0014> produced by the reflection principle has the property that given <MATH_0015> the reduction of <MATH_0016> is also an object of <MATH_0017> (left as an exercise).
